title: Gaming Platforms and Hardware/Software Co-design
purpose: Study boards, memory, GPU architecture, performance, input/display pipelines and integrated design.

modules.title: Embedded platforms, drivers and board design
modules.prerequisites: Modules 17-18 and 31-35. Physical work remains optional and supervised.
modules.project: Design a simulated controller or peripheral with firmware, a host interface and a schematic-level review. A physical board extension begins only after the electrical, layout and bring-up plans receive qualified review.

lessons.title: Serial interfaces and peripheral contracts
lessons.outcome: Choose a communication interface using timing and electrical constraints.
lessons.practical_assignment: Build a simulated peripheral transaction decoder and driver for one interface. Pass: incorrect framing or mode is detected, timeouts are bounded and a complete interface-contract table is provided.
lessons.assigned_reading: R53: device drivers, UART, SPI and I2C APIs; R51: bus-level driver documentation. For hardware, add the exact peripheral datasheet.
original_quiz: Why can two SPI devices fail at the same clock rate?
Does an interface name guarantee voltage compatibility?
Why begin with one interface rather than every bus?

lessons.title: Firmware, RTOS scheduling and driver lifecycle
lessons.outcome: Bound embedded work and make device state transitions explicit.
lessons.practical_assignment: Use a supported RTOS simulator or a deterministic scheduler model to implement input, processing and logging tasks. Pass: deadlines are evaluated under injected load and removal/cancellation leaves no live invalid requests.
lessons.assigned_reading: R53: kernel scheduling, synchronization and device model; R51: driver lifecycle and power management.
original_quiz: Does an RTOS automatically make all tasks meet deadlines?
Why not feed a watchdog unconditionally from a stuck loop?
What must happen to outstanding requests when a device disappears?

lessons.title: Schematics, PCB layout, power integrity and signal integrity
lessons.outcome: Translate a circuit into a manufacturable layout without ignoring physics.
lessons.practical_assignment: Create a low-speed peripheral schematic and unrouted or simple two-layer layout in KiCad. Pass: footprints are checked against datasheets, ERC/DRC findings are resolved or justified and a reviewer inspects power and return paths before fabrication.
lessons.assigned_reading: R36: schematic editor, PCB editor, ERC and DRC; R30: nonideal circuit behavior; R49: interconnect and packaging extension.
original_quiz: Does passing DRC prove electrical correctness?
Why do return paths matter?
Why verify footprints against datasheets?

lessons.title: Bring-up, instrumentation and fault isolation
lessons.outcome: Turn an unresponsive device into a sequence of testable hypotheses.
lessons.practical_assignment: Write and rehearse a bring-up procedure against a simulated device with injected clock, reset and protocol faults. Pass: each fault has a safe diagnostic branch and the procedure includes explicit stop conditions.
lessons.assigned_reading: R53: board support and debugging; R36: fabrication outputs and design review; selected instrument manuals for any physical extension.
original_quiz: Why test power, clock and reset before complex application behavior?
What is the value of an expected-observation table?
What should happen when a physical observation exceeds a reviewed safe limit?

modules.title: GPU microarchitecture and memory systems
modules.project: Create a GPU architecture workbook connecting shader behavior to execution groups, registers, memory transactions and fixed-function resources. Measure one accessible GPU or clearly label a simulator-only study.

lessons.title: SIMT execution, divergence, occupancy and latency hiding
lessons.outcome: Explain why many threads do not guarantee useful parallel work.
lessons.practical_assignment: Compare coherent and divergent workloads, varying register pressure or group size where supported. Pass: outputs agree, device group assumptions are recorded and the report does not equate occupancy with performance.
lessons.assigned_reading: R37: programming model, execution and hardware implementation; R48: vector and multithreaded architecture foundations.
original_quiz: What is branch divergence in grouped GPU execution?
Does high occupancy guarantee high throughput?
Why can reducing register use sometimes hurt?

lessons.title: Coalescing, local storage, caches and shared-memory banks
lessons.outcome: Match data layout to the memory transactions actually performed.
lessons.practical_assignment: Benchmark contiguous, strided and tiled access with identical useful work. Pass: count useful bytes, state the relevant memory level and include any layout-conversion cost in the application comparison.
lessons.assigned_reading: R37: device memory access, shared memory and performance considerations; R43: operational intensity.
original_quiz: What does coalescing improve?
Why can shared memory still cause stalls?
Why include layout conversion in a comparison?

lessons.title: Raster, texture, matrix and ray-tracing units
lessons.outcome: Understand fixed-function acceleration as specialized tradeoffs.
lessons.practical_assignment: Analyze one texture-heavy, arithmetic-heavy or ray-query workload. Pass: identify the likely resource limits using measurements or a documented model and state supported precision and feature assumptions.
lessons.assigned_reading: R37: architecture and specialized operations; R21: graphics/compute capabilities; R23: ray intersection and acceleration reference.
original_quiz: Does a ray-tracing unit eliminate the rest of rendering work?
Why compare the same numerical precision or quality?
When might specialized hardware lose on a small workload?

lessons.title: CPU-GPU sharing, discrete memory and synchronization
lessons.outcome: Treat shared addressability separately from ownership and cost.
lessons.practical_assignment: Compare an upload/compute/readback path with an available shared-memory path, or model both with stated assumptions. Pass: correct ownership, separate phase timings and no claim that unified means zero-cost.
lessons.assigned_reading: R37: memory management and synchronization; R21, R24 or R25: the selected platform's resource-sharing contract.
original_quiz: Does shared addressing mean zero data-access cost?
Why is CPU modification during GPU use risky?
What must an end-to-end accelerator benchmark include?

modules.title: Quantitative performance engineering
modules.project: Produce a performance investigation with a hypothesis, controlled workload, raw measurements, uncertainty, a bottleneck model and a verified optimization. A negative result is acceptable when the evidence is rigorous.

lessons.title: Amdahl, roofline and bottleneck models
lessons.outcome: Use upper bounds to reject implausible optimization claims.
lessons.practical_assignment: Build a roofline worksheet for one kernel and an Amdahl estimate for one frame optimization. Pass: units cancel correctly, modeled ceilings use the declared memory level and observed deviations are explained as hypotheses.
lessons.assigned_reading: R43: original Roofline model; R48: quantitative architecture; revisit Module 18 parallel limits.
original_quiz: What is the example roofline bound?
What is the maximum speedup with 20% unchanged serial work and infinitely fast remaining work?
Does being below the roof prove the model is wrong?

lessons.title: Profilers, counters and trustworthy benchmark design
lessons.outcome: Distinguish observation from an explanation that still needs testing.
lessons.practical_assignment: Create a benchmark harness with warmup, repeated runs, output validation and metadata. Pass: an intentional no-op or wrong-result variant is rejected and all included/excluded samples are documented.
lessons.assigned_reading: R26: profiling; R37: performance analysis; R09: inference and uncertainty.
original_quiz: Why validate benchmark output?
Are similarly named counters identical across all processors?
Why declare an exclusion policy before inspecting results?

lessons.title: SIMD, cache blocking, NUMA and job scheduling
lessons.outcome: Optimize locality and parallelism together.
lessons.practical_assignment: Optimize a particle or transform workload using one locality change and one scheduling change. Pass: test tail sizes, report numerical differences, and measure small as well as large workloads to expose overhead.
lessons.assigned_reading: R37: parallel memory patterns; R48: multiprocessors and memory systems; R11: safe C++ and concurrency.
original_quiz: What is false sharing?
Why can very small jobs be inefficient?
Why test small workloads after a parallel optimization?

lessons.title: Energy, thermal behavior and sustained performance
lessons.outcome: Evaluate useful work over time rather than only a short peak.
lessons.practical_assignment: Run a sustained workload within normal device limits or analyze a synthetic power trace. Pass: distinguish watts from joules, report the measurement boundary and compare early versus sustained performance.
lessons.assigned_reading: R48: quantitative architecture; R51: device power management; R37: GPU execution and performance context.
original_quiz: How much energy is 50 W for 2 seconds?
Which example uses less task energy?
Why not disable thermal protections for a curriculum benchmark?

modules.title: Gaming-platform constraints and interactive latency
modules.project: Create a platform capability and latency report for the engine. Implement one non-desktop constraint in simulation or on an available device: touch input, suspend/resume, restricted memory, variable presentation or XR timing.

lessons.title: Input-to-display latency and frame pacing
lessons.outcome: Account for the whole interaction path rather than only frame rate.
lessons.practical_assignment: Instrument input receipt, simulation consumption, render submission and presentation-related timestamps. Pass: explain which stages are actually measured and which remain estimated, and show a frame-pacing distribution.
lessons.assigned_reading: R22: input and event timing; R24 or R25: presentation; R52: frame timing as an advanced comparison.
original_quiz: Is 60 frames per second a complete latency measurement?
What is two 60 Hz frame intervals?
Why label timestamp boundaries precisely?

lessons.title: Mobile and handheld systems: memory, power and lifecycle
lessons.outcome: Design for suspension, limited budgets and sustained use.
lessons.practical_assignment: Add suspend/resume simulation and a constrained memory mode. Pass: progress survives the documented lifecycle, resources are restored safely and quality changes do not alter authoritative simulation rules.
lessons.assigned_reading: R25: platform graphics resources; R22: application lifecycle events; R29: text and input usability; R51: power-management concepts.
original_quiz: Why not assume shutdown always provides unlimited save time?
Why measure sustained rather than only initial performance?
What should rendering quality tiers preserve?

lessons.title: XR spaces, stereo views, pose timing and comfort constraints
lessons.outcome: Render from runtime-provided timing and coordinate contracts.
lessons.practical_assignment: Implement two simulated camera views and a pose-time log, or a minimal OpenXR scene on available supported hardware. Pass: spaces and units are explicit, frame timing follows the runtime and loss of tracking has defined behavior.
lessons.assigned_reading: R52: spaces, view configuration, frame loop and timing; R29: interaction and accessibility review.
original_quiz: Why is a pose incomplete without a space and time?
Should stereo projection be hard-coded for every headset?
Does prediction remove all latency or discomfort risk?

lessons.title: Portability, platform services and console-development boundaries
lessons.outcome: Build transferable systems without assuming proprietary access.
lessons.practical_assignment: Write a platform interface and capability matrix, then implement a second backend or strict mock. Pass: assumptions about paths, input and lifecycle are exposed, and proprietary requirements are marked unavailable until authorized.
lessons.assigned_reading: R22, R24 and R25: platform interfaces; R29: cross-device usability; official authorized platform documentation only for restricted targets.
original_quiz: Why can a strict mock help portability?
Does public self-study grant access to proprietary console SDKs?
Why separate packaged assets from persistent saves?

modules.title: Hardware/software co-design capstone
modules.project: Gate H: choose one game workload and compare a software baseline with a specialized hardware or architecture alternative. Deliver a reference implementation, model or RTL, software interface, verification evidence and an end-to-end tradeoff report.

lessons.title: Workload characterization and measurable requirements
lessons.outcome: Derive hardware goals from a real software operation.
lessons.practical_assignment: Select a workload from the engine and write a requirement sheet plus baseline measurements. Pass: each target has units and a test, and the maximum plausible application benefit is estimated.
lessons.assigned_reading: R43: bottleneck modeling; R48: quantitative design; R49: project methodology.
original_quiz: Why start with workload measurements?
What maximum fraction of the example frame can removing 0.2 ms save?
Can rejecting a hardware proposal be a successful outcome?

lessons.title: Architecture alternatives, arithmetic precision and dataflow
lessons.outcome: Explore several designs before committing to one.
lessons.practical_assignment: Model three variants, such as scalar, pipelined and multi-lane. Pass: resource and bandwidth estimates are explicit, fixed-point error meets a chosen application tolerance and rejected variants have documented reasons.
lessons.assigned_reading: R49: architecture and RTL modeling; R43: bandwidth limits; R33: resource inference.
original_quiz: Why might twice as many lanes fail to double throughput?
What should determine acceptable quantization error?
Why explore more than one architecture?

lessons.title: Interface design, virtualization and end-to-end evaluation
lessons.outcome: Include the host software in the hardware result.
lessons.practical_assignment: Implement a host driver model with invalid-descriptor, timeout and reset tests. Pass: buffer bounds are enforced, ownership survives failure and results include both kernel and end-to-end timing.
lessons.assigned_reading: R51: DMA and device interfaces; R49: system integration; R38: modeled systems when hardware is unavailable.
original_quiz: Why validate device work descriptors?
Can kernel and application speedups legitimately differ?
Why test realistic batch sizes?

lessons.title: Design review, evidence tiers and undergraduate CE completion
lessons.outcome: Defend a co-design decision with limitations and reproducible artifacts.
lessons.practical_assignment: Complete Gate H and a design-review presentation. Pass: every major claim traces to an artifact, the baseline is reproduced and a limitations section clearly separates educational estimates from production claims.
lessons.assigned_reading: R49: design-project reporting; R48: architectural tradeoffs; revisit the evidence and project rubrics in the handbook.
original_quiz: Why label simulation and physical measurements separately?
What makes a baseline competent?
Does Gate H authorize production chip fabrication?

gate_spec.title: undergraduate hardware/software co-design capstone
gate_spec.requirements_markdown:
**After Volume 8.** Choose one measured engine workload. Compare a competent software baseline with at least two architecture alternatives, implementing one alternative as RTL, a supported simulation model or a bounded analytical prototype with clear limitations.

Required evidence includes workload distributions, numerical-quality limits, host/device ownership, setup and transfer costs, resource/timing estimates, failure handling and a sensitivity analysis. Evaluate small and large workloads and one adverse case. A negative conclusion is acceptable: proving that a software optimization is preferable is valid co-design work.

The review must identify the maximum application benefit, the dominant bottleneck, which results are modeled and which are measured, and what changes under a tighter memory or latency constraint. Do not compare an optimized accelerator against an intentionally weak software baseline.
